content: Essential medicines, as defined by the World Health Organization (WHO), are those drugs that meet the healthcare needs of the majority of the population. These medicines must be available at all times in sufficient quantities, in appropriate dosage forms, and at a price that is affordable to the community. The WHO has developed a model list of essential medicines, which serves as a guideline for countries to create their own lists based on local healthcare priorities. This model list is divided into two categories: the core list and the complementary list. The core list includes the minimum set of medicines required for a basic healthcare system. These medicines are selected based on their proven efficacy, safety, and cost-effectiveness in treating priority health conditions. Priority conditions are identified based on their current and projected public health significance, as well as the potential for safe and cost-effective treatment. The complementary list, on the other hand, includes essential medicines for priority diseases that require specialized diagnostic or monitoring facilities. Medicines may also be included in the complementary list if they are associated with consistently higher costs or if their cost-effectiveness is less favorable in various healthcare settings. The creation of an essential medicines list allows health authorities, particularly in developing countries, to optimize the allocation and use of pharmaceutical resources.
